'''Muhammad Aurangzeb Ahmad''' is an American computer scientist and an assistant professor at [[Baylor College of Medicine]].<ref name="bcm" /><ref name="atlas" /> His research covers artificial intelligence in healthcare, [[Responsible AI]], and [[Digital immortality|digital afterlife]]. Ahmad built '''Grandpa Bot''', one of the earliest examples of griefbots.<ref name="cbc2018" /><ref name="pbs2023" /><ref name="ars2025will" /><ref name="bbc2026" />

== Early life and education ==
Ahmad earned a bachelor's degree in computer science from the [[Rochester Institute of Technology]] in 2006, where he also studied philosophy,<ref name="rit2021" /> and received an honorable mention in the [[Computing Research Association]]'s 2006 Outstanding Undergraduate Research Award.<ref name="cra2006" /> He received a Ph.D. in computer science from the [[University of Minnesota]] in 2011 with a dissertation on computational trust.<ref name="mgp" /> This research contributed to the launch of a game-analytics startup.<ref name="umnstartup" /><ref name="about" />

== Career ==
Ahmad held positions in applied AI in various industries <ref name="aifaith" /><ref name="geekwire2017" /><ref name="about" /> before moving into healthcare AI at various startups, [[Boston Scientific]], and at [[Kaiser Permanente]].<ref name="aifaith" /><ref name="about" /> He held affiliate faculty appointments in computer science at the University of Washington, [[University of Washington Bothell|UW Bothell]],<ref name="aifaith" /><ref name="uwb2025" /> and was a research fellow in the Department of Surgery at [[Harborview Medical Center]]<ref name="uwb2025" /><ref name="escience" /> and affiliated faculty with UW's Responsible AI Systems and Experiences initiative.<ref name="about" /> {{As of|2026}}, he is an assistant professor of surgery at [[Baylor College of Medicine]] and a member of its ATLAS A.I. research program.<ref name="bcm" /><ref name="atlas" />

== Research ==
Ahmad's early research was in [[computational social science]], particularly the analysis of behavior and social networks in online games.<ref name="mgp" /><ref name="goldfarm2009" /> Since the mid-2010s his work has focused mainly on artificial intelligence in healthcare.<ref name="uwb2025" /><ref name="escience" /><ref name="about" />

=== Computational social science ===
Ahmad's early research used behavioral data from the [[MMORPG]]s. With his colleagues he carried out one of the first systematic studies of automatically detecting "[[Gold farming|gold farmers]]", players who illicitly gather virtual goods to sell for real money, and filed a patent application for the method.<ref name="goldfarm2009" /><ref name="patent2012" /> The group found that gold farmers' networks were structurally similar to real-world drug-trafficking networks,<ref name="darkgold2010" /><ref name="xrds2011" /><ref name="kotaku2010" /><ref name="escapist2010" /><ref name="boing2010" /> and that farmers trusted highly central ordinary players but not one another.<ref name="rogues2011" /> Papers from the project won best paper awards in 2011 at the ACM Web Science Conference and at the Game Behind the Video Game conference at [[Rutgers University]].<ref name="keeganvita" /><ref name="sonic2011" /> 

=== Healthcare artificial intelligence ===
Ahmad's healthcare research covers clinical prediction, including mortality, critical care and hospital operations,<ref name="aaai2018" /><ref name="ichi2021icu" /><ref name="ichi2023" /> and responsible AI.<ref name="bcb2018" /><ref name="ichi2021fair" /><ref name="kdd2021" /><ref name="suc2023" /> He helped develop and prospectively validate various predictive models,<ref name="readmit2019" /> has worked on hallucination mitigation in medical language models,<ref name="llm2023" /> and led the team that created fairMLHealth, an open-source toolkit for assessing bias in clinical models.<ref name="fairml" /> He has also led research on AI "surrogates" to estimate the treatment preferences of incapacitated patients. He has argued that they should reflect a patient's values and remain transparent decision aids rather than decision makers.<ref name="arxiv2025" /><ref name="forbes2025" /> The project tests whether models trained on patients' injury severity, medical history and prior choices can predict their treatment preferences, with accuracy checked against the stated wishes of patients who later recover.<ref name="ars2025surrogate" /><ref name="forbes2025" />

=== Digital afterlife and Grandpa Bot ===
After his father died in 2013, Ahmad built a conversational simulation of him, mainly so that his future children could know their grandfather.<ref name="uwb2025" /><ref name="ars2025will" /> The chatbot became known as Grandpa Bot.<ref name="uwb2025" /><ref name="cbc2018" /><ref name="fox2025" /><ref name="larazon2017" /><ref name="indianexpress2019" /><ref name="beast2018" /><ref name="indy2018" /><ref name="discover2024" /><ref name="flashforward2019" /> The project<ref name="chi2016" /> has been included as one of the few studies to address their effects on children;<ref name="jimenez2023" /><ref name="hollanek2024" /> the [[Markkula Center for Applied Ethics]] used the project as the basis for a 2018 ethics case study.<ref name="markkula2018" /> ''Ars Technica'' described Ahmad as one of the first AI researchers to build a grief bot.<ref name="ars2025will" /> He has warned that such systems could displace real relationships.<ref name="uwb2025" /><ref name="komo2025" />

=== AI ethics ===
Ahmad has also worked on AI ethics and governance. <ref name="oneonline2019" /><ref name="un2025" /> He helped create "Rabbi Bot", a chatbot trained on a Houston rabbi's sermons,<ref name="ucdavis2026" /> which ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported was used to write and deliver a sermon in the rabbi's cloned voice.<ref name="nyt2025" />. ''[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]'' included him among Muslim scholars and technologists examining how Islamic ethics can inform the development and use of artificial intelligence.<ref name="wired2021">{{cite magazine |last=Ahuja |first=Sparsh |date=January 25, 2021 |title=Muslim scholars are working to reconcile Islam and AI |url=https://www.wired.com/story/islamic-ai/ |access-date=October 4, 2026 |magazine=Wired}}</ref>
